mya: ciinkweensa peenaalinta piolinki, eehonci peewaaliaki pyaawaaci,
en: Ciinkweensa was born in Paola, where the Peorias came from,

mya: niišomatene yaalanwaasi pipoonwe aawiki.
en: twenty-five years ago.

mya: eehkwi peewaaliaki aancihseewaahsiikwi,
en: Before the Peorias emigrated,

mya: oonaana ciinkweensa neekalaata ooneehi peewaaliaki.
en: Ciinkweensa had left the Peorias.

mya: weeteemaata kiikaapwahi.
en: He went with some Kickapoos.

mya: neehi meehci peewaaliaki aancihseewaaci,
en: And after the Peorias had moved,

mya: niišwi pipoonwe meehci-hka,
en: two years later,

mya: ciinkweensa eeweemaacihi awiila atašiihkiomi ciikaahkwe piolinki eetaaweeciki.
en: Ciinkweensa’s relatives sold his land near Paola.

mya: iišiteeheewaaci, awiila-hsa neepiki.
en: They thought that he had died.

mya: maankoohkwa neehi oona ciinkwaahkia awiilwa meeyayohsiwaaci eeweemaawaaci toki ciinkweensali.
en: Maankoohkwa and Ciinkwaahkia claimed to be relatives of Ciinkweensa.

mya: ooniini wiiyoonkonci awiilwa eetaaweeciki awiila atašiihkiomi.
en: Because of this, they sold his land.

mya: nkoti pipoonwe meehci eetaaweewaaci ooniini ašiihkiwi, maamawi awiilwa neepikiki caaciikaahkwe.
en: One year after they had sold that land, they both died close together.

mya: kiinšimi meehci niiloona waahi pyaayaanki, wiihsa peewaliaki nakaani neepikiki.
en: Soon after we arrived here, many of the older Peorias passed away.

mya: mataathswi nkotaasi pipoonwe meehci aancihsiaanki waahi, oonaana ciinkweensa pyaata aapwe oowaanci kiikaaponkonci.
en: Eleven years after we had moved here, Ciinkweensa returned from being with the Kickapoos.

mya: moohci nkoti kihkeelimeehsiiwa awiila, kiinte keeloosici peewaalia iilaataweenki.
en: Not a single person knew who he was, until he started speaking the Peoria language.

mya: iilaapantanici maaci mayaawi kotakinkiši oowaanci peewaaliahi iini aawiki.
en: He looked very different from the Peorias who were living around here at that time.

mya: naapinanka awiila waapimotayi neehpikanki, meehcihkiita, weehkweetiita ataahsema neehi mahkisina, moohci atehtolenihsiiwa.
en: He wore a red blanket, he was bare-headed, he wore leggings and moccasins, and he did not wear a hat.

mya: piilaata awiiwali kiikaapwa.
en: He brought his Kickapoo wife.

mya: mitemhsa awiila neepika, neehi noohki eewiiyomita peewaalia mitemhsa, ileeši ahseehsiiwaki moohci piloohsahi.
en: The woman died, and he got remarried to a Peoria woman, but they did not have any children.

mya: wiihsa piilaata neekatikašiahi.
en: He brought several horses.

mya: ceeki eetaaweeta kihcitawe niišwi peemawalaacihi.
en: He sold all of them except two dray horses.

mya: awiila atašiihkiomi eetaaweenki kotakaki aweeyaki.
en: His land had already been sold by others.

mya: neehi awiila eetaaweeta noohki niiwi cimiinawa yaalanwi mihtekowalaakani.
en: And then he sold it again for four or five thousand dollars.

mya: meehci eehtooki ooniini šooli iiyaata seenikionkiši.
en: After he got this money he went to Seneca.

mya: meemaata iilahosiwaaci keekaanohšiahi, neehi nkoti ahkihkiwahkihkwa moohkine wiiški.
en: He bought a team of mules and one clay jug full of whiskey.

mya: meehci maaciihkaaci awiikinkiši eehinki miiyonki, kipahkaakani ahkihkiwahkikonki peehsikohkaaki neehi kweelotanki.
en: After he started off down the road for home, the stopper on the jug came loose and he lost it.

mya: nihswi cimiinawa niiwaahkwe ciika kiipalwahwaaci ahkihkiwahkihkooli ooni šooli.
en: He stopped up the jug with nearly three or four hundred dollars of the money.

mya: awiila šooli meehci ceekihpenatooki, aapweeyaata kiikaaponkiši.
en: After he had spent all his money, he went back to the Kickapoos.

mya: neepiki kiinšimi meehci neehpyaaci niiyaaha.
en: He died soon after he got there.

mya: maaliaani awiiwali milohta awiila neepika.
en: His wife Mary Ann died before him.

mya: niiyaaha aawiki 1866 ciinkweensa neekalaata weeci-mihtohseeniyomaacihi.
en: Around 1866 Ciinkweensa left the people he had been living with.

mya: kiikaponkiši iiyaata, kiikaapohkwiali weekimaata, neehi aapwe pyaaci peewaaliaki.
en: He went to Kickapoo country, married a Kickapoo woman, and came back to the Peorias.

mya: neehi aapwe neepakiminta peewaaliaki.
en: Then he was counted as a member of the Peorias again.

mya: akimahi kweecimolikota, “taanaaha ntaahswi kiniicaanhsaki eehsaci?”
en: Then the chiefs asked him, “How many children do you have?”

mya: “palaani niniicaanhsaki”, iišiweeta.
en: “I have eight children”, he said.

mya: akimaki neepihšimaaciki, neehi naahpi šooli miilinciki.
en: The chiefs put him on the roll, and they also were given money.

mya: aapweeyaata kiikaaponkiši neehi nihsenwi, toki miinawa niiyanwi eehkoleeciki.
en: He went back to the Kickapoos and three or four times they made payments (to him).

mya: meehciweele meehkoonta, kilaahkiihkici-hsa.
en: Afterwards he was found to have lied.

mya: nkoti-hsa teehši eehsaaci piloohsali.
en: He really only had one child.

mya: aapwe iiyaata kiikaaponkiši.
en: He went back to the Kickapoos.

mya: nkotenwi-hsa mihšihkatokaawaaci kiikaapooki aleniaki.
en: Once, some Kickapoo men were having a war dance.

mya: tawaani peekantankiki eehi eeteehsiyokaawaaci.
en: They were striking the post, where they were doing the warrior dance.

mya: ciinkweensa ihsa peekantanki tawaani ahpwaakani, eeyoowaaci aalinta maalhsi.
en: Ciinkweensa then struck the post with a pipe-tomahawk, while some others were using a knife.

mya: neehi-hsa ciinkweensa naalaahkwaahkici maalhsi, peehkišanki pakwantioni.
en: And then Ciinkweensa pulled out a knife, cutting his belt in two.

mya: neehi-hsa akootayi paapintenki.
en: His breechcloth fell down.

mya: neehi-hsa aleniaki keeweešinoonci, paapaakahamoowaaci anehkawe.
en: He was laughed at by the men, and they clapped their hands.

mya: nkotenwi-hsa mihšihkatokaawaaci kiikaapooki aleniaki.
en: Once, some Kickapoo men were having a war dance.

mya: tawaani peekantankiki eehi eeteehsiyokaawaaci.
en: They were striking the post, where they were doing the warrior dance.

mya: ciinkweensa ihsa peekantanki tawaani ahpwaakani, eeyoowaaci aalinta maalhsi.
en: Ciinkweensa then struck the post with a pipe-tomahawk, while some others were using a knife.

mya: neehi-hsa ciinkweensa naalaahkwaahkici maalhsi, peehkišanki pakwantioni.
en: And then Ciinkweensa pulled out a knife, cutting his belt in two.

mya: neehi-hsa akootayi paapintenki.
en: His breechcloth fell down.

mya: neehi-hsa aleniaki keeweešinoonci, paapaakahamoowaaci anehkawe.
en: He was laughed at by the men, and they clapped their hands.

mya: wiihsakacaakwa-hsa peempaalici ciikaahkwe siipionki.
en: Wiihsakacaakwa was walking along near a river.

mya: neehi-hsa meehkohkawaaci meehtikoošiali.
en: And then he came upon a Frenchman.

mya: “pažo, pažo, pažo!” naawi aašawišiweelici mootaakani.
en: “Bon jour, bon jour, bon jour!” (he said). He was going around to trade some merchandise.

mya: iilaata: “taaniši ayaayani?”
en: He asked him, “Where are you going?”

mya: iilikoci-hsa: “teepi-nko-hka weeteemilaani kimehsoleminki?”
en: (Wiihsakacaakwa) said, “Can I go with you in your boat?”

mya: “iihiye, wiiteemilo!”
en: (The Frenchman answered him), “yes, come with me”.

mya: “ahkawaahilo namehka! paala-hka nintankihaa eehsipana, neehihka nimpaahswaa.”
en: “Wait for me a bit! First, I have to kill a raccoon, and then dry it.”

mya: neehi-hsa pootaweeci koteewi, wiila-hka paahswaaci eehsipana.
en: And then he started a fire, to dry the raccoon (hide).

mya: neehi-hsa meehci paahswaata eekintanki ntaahswi kiihkaapiikihsenki ansooyinki.
en: And then after he dried it, he counted the number of rings going around its tail.

mya: neehi, “eekami kiikaapiikhsenki ansooyinki, nkoti kiikoo miilinki”, iišiteeheeci-hsa.
en: And, “For each ring going around the tail, I’ll be given one item”, he thought.

mya: ahkolayi, neehi waapimotayi, neehi papikwani, neehi mahkateewi, neehi aloonhsa.
en: A cape, a blanket, a gun, gunpowder, and some bullets.

mya: teepiihsiinwi! noohki kati nintankihaa moohswa.
en: But it’s not enough! Next I’ll kill a deer.

mya: neehi-hsa eenkihaata ayaapeenhsali.
en: And so he killed a young buck.

mya: wiihsa keetakisilici.
en: It had spots all over it.

mya: hwi, hwi! wiihsa kati kiikoo nimame aašawišiwiaani, paakweeci wiihsa keetakisita nimoohswayema.
en: Ha ha! I’ll get a lot for my deerskin when I trade it, what with these spots all over it!

mya: iihi, nimpoosi kati kimehsoleminki.
en: Alright, I’ll get in your boat.

mya: neehi-hsa maaciihkaawaaci ataaweelenikaanionkiši.
en: And they started off towards the trading post.

mya: neehi-hsa taahtakiihšinki mihsoolinki neehineeci.
en: And then (Wiihsakacaakwa) laid down in the boat singing.

mya: “paakišiinkweelo, niihka! eemamowia ciikaahkwe wiiyaahkiwa. noontoohke kati kimamikona”, iilikota meehtikoošiali.
en: “Be quiet, my friend, the man-eater lives nearby! If he hears you, he’ll catch us!” the Frenchman said.

mya: wiihsakacaakwa ihsa leni noontawaahsiikwi. eehinki iišinaakiici- hsa.
en: Wiihsakacaakwa didn’t seem to hear him. He sang that way to the end.

mya: kiihtile-hsa noontaakowaaci manetoowali.
en: Sure enough, the Manitou heard them.

mya: neehi-hsa meemikowaaci peentikiihsaawaaci.
en: Then he caught them, and they fell into (his den).

mya: meehtikoošia seehkweeci.
en: The Frenchman wept.

mya: wiihsakacaakwa waawaapantanki ceeki kiikoo.
en: Wiihsakacaakwa looked everything over.

mya: neehi-hsa-hkwa: “taaniswi? taaniswi?” iilaaci ihsa-hkwa.
en: Again and again, “How much? How much?”, he said, again and again.

mya: neehi-hsa keelolekohsiikwi swaahteethswintepikanka manetoowali.
en: The seven-headed manitou would not answer him.

mya: tikawi kweehsikoci manetoowali.
en: The manitou was a little afraid of him.

mya: kapootwe-hsa eeyiihkwici wiihsakacaakwa.
en: After a while, Wiihsakacaakwa got hungry.

mya: “hungry, hungry! nisimina, kiinaka, niihka, oolawi-hkwa ataaweeliniaki ahšaliwaki”.
en: “Hungry! Hungry! We say, damn it, my friend, the shop-keepers ought to feed people”.

mya: neehi-hsa manetoowali: “akwaniinkweehamooko kiiyoowe!”
en: And then the Manitou (said), “Cover your faces!”

mya: neehi-hsa ceeki eekwanahamoowaata awiiyoowe waapimotayi.
en: And they all covered themselves with a blanket.

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa ahkolayi poohkahki.
en: And Wiihsakacaakwa’s cape had a hole in it.

mya: niiyaancihsa keemaapamaaci.
en: He secretly watched them through it.

mya: naahpa-hsa ntaahswi pahkihteepineelici.
en: But a number of them were starving.

mya: mihtohseeniahi ihsa eemwaalici.
en: (The manitou) ate the people up.

mya: neehi-hsa meehci weehsineelici, aapwe: “paahkiinkweehšinooko!”
en: And then, after he ate, he contined: “Uncover your faces!”

mya: kapootwe keetankwaanki manetoowa.
en: After a while the Manitou became sleepy.

mya: neehi-hsa ceenkwankeepici.
en: Then, when he sat down, he made a great rumbling noise.

mya: ašiihkiwi naanaamaamihkiiki.
en: The earth shook.

mya: neehi-hsa weešihšinki.
en: He laid down.

mya: noonkaaha-hka “nipeewa” iišiteeheeci wiihsakacaakwa. peesikwiihsaaci-hsa. naanaamaahkiici-hsa ceeki swaahteethswi antepikana. aalweelici-hsa kati amatinaaci.
en: At that point, Wiihsakacaakwa thought “he’s asleep”. He sprang up. He shook all seven of (the Manitou’s) heads. He couldn’t wake (the Manitou) up.

mya: neehi-hsa paahkinanki mahkateewa teepantaakanhsenki. seehsiikinanki antepikaninki manetoowali. neehi-hsa ceeki: “noontiohseeko!” aalinta naawi peehkihteepineewaaci. aalweeliwaaci ihsa kati noontiohseewaaci.
en: And so then he opened a keg of gunpowder. He poured it out onto the Manitou’s heads. And to all (the captives), he said “get out!” Some were almost starved. They couldn’t get out.

mya: ceeki kiikoo ntaahswi mihsawinanki ihsa meenki awiila.
en: He took as much as he wanted of everything.

mya: neehi-hsa naanameekinki meehkatiaapiikinanki.
en: And then he rubbed gunpowder into a rag.

mya: neehi-hsa antepikaninkonci ahkwaanteeminkiši iilaapiikatooki.
en: And he strung it out away from their heads, towards the door.

mya: neehi-hsa noontiohseeci. šaakosanki mahkatiaapiikwi. saakaciweeci-hsa. pihkwaahkionkonci waapantanki eehi-pankiswaaci manetoowali.
en: Then he got out. He lit the fuse. Then he emerged. From a hilltop he watched where he was going to blow the manitou up.

mya: meehci peenkiswaaci, teepeentaahswi-pipoonwe ihsa weenteeki nipi.
en: After he blew him up, the water boiled for a period of time.

mya: sakaanki teehkihsenki. neehi-hsa aapwe peentikiita.
en: Eventually, it cooled off. And he went back in.

mya: šeekwihtooki manetoowa awiiki.
en: He took possession of the manitou’s home.

mya: awiila noonki teepeelintanki.
en: Now he owned it.

mya: meehci ceeki noontiaahkiici ciipaya ahkana neehi manetoowa ahkana.
en: Later, (Wiihsakacaakwa) threw out all the corpses’ bones and the manitou’s bones.

mya: teetankonanki. neehaahkitooki kati niiya wiiyaahkici.
en: He cleaned it out. He made it nice, so as to live there.

mya: neehi nkoti kaahkiihkwe noontiohseeci.
en: Then one day he came out.

mya: neehi aahsansici meehcikilita ahsena.
en: And he sunned himself on a large rock.

mya: niiyaaha taahtakiihšinki.
en: He was lying down there.

mya: neehi-hsa neewaaci payiihsahi.
en: Then he saw some dwarves.

mya: pyaalici eehi waakihsenki siipiiwi.
en: They were coming from where there was a bend in the river.

mya: aacimwi neepaaci. “taaniši toki kati išiliniwaaci?”, iišiteeheeci.
en: He pretended to be asleep. “I wonder what they’ll do?”, he thought.

mya: neehi-hsa payiihsaki iilitiiwaaci, “naawa wiihsakacaakwa, nipeewa ahseninki. seekihaahkaawi!” neehi-hsa kookiiwaaci nipinki. ciikaahkwe moohkiiwaaci ahsenaali. neehi-hsa nkoti: “niila kati nimpemwaa”.
en: And then the dwarves said to each another, “There’s Wiihsakacaakwa, asleep on a rock. Let’s scare him!” And they dove into the water. Near a rock they emerged. Then one (said), “I’ll shoot him”.

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa noontawaaci. “eehkwa kiinaka! mihsawinameekwe, wiihkotamawihsiiweekwi. miililakakoki-hka”.
en: And Wiihsakacaakwa heard him. “Hold it, damn it! If you want (the cave), (why) didn’t you ask me for it? I’d give it to you”.

mya: neehi: “meehsawinamaanki” iilikoci payiihsahi.
en: Then the dwarves said, “we want it”.

mya: “niiši, niihi išimihsiiweekwi teehši pimoweeyoni? poonamoolakoki kati, neehi-hka maaciihkaani”.
en: “Well, anyway, (why) didn’t you tell me, instead of shooting? I’ll give it up to you, and then I’ll be on my way.”

mya: neehi-hsa payiihsaki teepeelintamoowaaci. eehkwa mihtelowe peepaamihkaweewaaci payiihsaki.
en: So then the dwarves became its owners. The footprints of the dwarves are still plainly visible.

mya: eehinki eehkwaapiikaasici wiihsakacaakwa.
en: That’s as far as Wiihsakacaakwa goes.

mya: wiihsakacaakwa ihsa peempaalici.
en: Wiihsakacaakwa was walking along.

mya: neehi-hsa meehkohkawaaci niišwi kiyošiaki keekiipiinkweewaaci. ceenkweepiwaaci seekinehkiinitiiwaaci.
en: Then he came across two old blind men. They were sitting down, holding onto each other’s hands.

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa peentikiici weekiwi awiikawe. neehi- hsa nkoti kiyošiali anehki peekamaaci. neehi-hsa kiyošiaki poonitiiwaaci.
en: Then Wiihsakacaakwa quietly entered their lodge. Then, he hit one of the old men with his hand. And the old men let go of each other.

mya: aapooši noohki kotakali kiyošiali peekamaaci anehki.
en: Once again, he hit the other old man with his hand.

mya: neehi-hsa nkoti kiyošia: “keetweenci kiila pakamiyani, niihka?” iilaata kotakali kiyošiali.
en: Then one old man said to the other old man, “Why are you hitting me, my friend?”

mya: neehi-hsa: “kiila mahtami peekamiyani!”
en: “You hit me first!”

mya: neehi-hsa ceeki peesikwiihsaawaaci. meekaalitiiwaaci.
en: And then they both jumped up. They started fighting.

mya: kapootwe-hsa nkoti aalaankweeci. “eehkwa, kiinaka, niihka. koohsemina kiinaka leni oowaaha wiiyaahkiwa”.
en: After a while, one of them got tired. “Hold on, damn it, my friend. It seems as though our grandchild is staying here”.

mya: neehi-hsa nkoti kiyošia iita: “kipwihsaace ahkwaanteemi.”
en: Then one of the old men said “Let the door slam shut”.

mya: neehi-hsa kiipwihsaaki ahkwaanteemi. wiihsakacaakwa kiipahonci. kiyošiaki neenatwahwaawaaci. kapootwe wiihsakacaakwa aalaankweeci. neehi-hsa seenaahkweeleešikoonci.
en: And then the door slammed shut. Wiihsakacaakwa was locked in. The old men punched around for him. After a while Wiihsakacaakwa got tired. And then he was cornered.

mya: “eehkwa! nimehšoominka, ankihihsooko! kitaahkohkinilemwa kati, kitaayaalimiihtoolimwa kati, ankihihsiiweekwe.”
en: “Hold it! My grandfathers, don’t kill me! I’ll wait on you and cook for you if you don’t kill me!”

mya: neehi-hsa kiyošiaki: “niiši ilweehsiiwani? niiši lehši paahpilotawiaanki. kiitimaakisiaanki, noohse”, iilinci-hsa wiihsakacaakwa.
en: Then the old men (said), “Why didn’t you say so? You made fun of us for no reason. We are poor and helpless, grandchild”, Wiihsakacaakwa was told.

mya: “iihiye, aayaalimiihtawiihkaanke, noohse”.
en: “Yes, you must cook for us, grandchild”.

mya: neehi-hsa niiyaaha weeyaahkici. weecikiimaaci kiyošiahi. aahkohkinaaci.
en: So there he stayed. He lived with the old men. He took care of them.

mya: kapootwe-hsa aahkwaahkiilimaaci kiyošiahi. neehi-hsa kati nakalaaci.
en: After a while, (Wiihsakacaakwa) got tired of the old men. And then he wanted to leave them.

mya: neehi kiyošiaki masaanaapiikwali nipinkiši iilaapiikalaawaaci, iši- hka waayowaahsiikwi nipi naatiwaaci. neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa kotakinkiši iilaapiikalaaci masaanaapiikwali eehiši kiihkatehkiki.
en: The old men had stretched ropes towards the water, so that they wouldn’t get lost when they went to fetch water. So Wiihsakacaakwa stretched out the ropes in the other direction, to where there was a steep bank.

mya: neehi-hsa maaciihkaaci. neekalaaci kiyošiahi.
en: And then he went away. He left the old men.

mya: kapootwe-hsa eeyiihkwiwaaci kiyošiaki.
en: After a while, the old men became hungry.

mya: neehi nkoti: “kiila, niihka, nipi naatilo! aalimiihtoohkaawi. koohsemina piici kinakalekona”.
en: And one said, “You, my friend, fetch some water! Let’s cook something. It looks like our grandchild has deserted us”.

mya: neehi-hsa nkoti kiyošia nipi naatiki. masaanaapiikwali weeyawaaci.
en: So one of the old men went to get water. He followed the rope.

mya: kiihtile paapincinki waahsatehkionkonci. neehi-hsa aalweelici kati kahkaciweeci aapwe. neehi-hsa naanoontaahkweeci awiihkaanali. neentomaaci.
en: Sure enough, he fell down the cliff. And he was unable to climb back up. And he shouted and shouted to his friend. He called him.

mya: neehi-hsa pyaalici. “weekiwi pyaalo! kipalihka kati! koohsemina ihsa kweehkaapiikihšimaaci masaanaapiikwali kotakinkiši”.
en: And then he came. (He said) “Be careful, you’ll slip! Our grandchild has rearranged the ropes in another direction.”

mya: neehi-hsa sakaanki masaanaapiikwali meehkonaaci. seekiinaaci nkoti kiyošia twaahkionki. neehi-hsa saakaciweeci aapwe. ceeki peentikiiwaaci awiikawaanki.
en: Then after a while he started to feel around for the ropes. The old man grabbed onto one, down in the hollows. And then he crawled back out. They both went into their lodge.

mya: neehi-hsa: “ataahpiswaataawi koohsemina wiihsakacaakwa”.
en: And then (one said): “Let’s draw our grandchild Wiihsakacaakwa by smoke”.

mya: neehi-hsa ahpwaakanali weelahkinalaawaaci. nkoti-hsa seehkahwaaci ahpwaakanali.
en: So they filled up the pipe. One of them lit the pipe.

mya: “niihka, ataahpiswi koohsemina. pakilaahkaawi pilowiši. aašihke wanimaahkaawi wiihsakacaakwa”.
en: He said, “My friend, draw our grandchild near. Let’s throw him far away. It’s our turn to fool Wiihsakacaakwa”.

mya: kiihtile aapwe waakohseeci. neehi pyaaci aapwe.
en: Sure enough, (Wiihsakacaakwa) circled back. And he returned.

mya: neehi-hsa kiyošiahi: “keetweenci kohkaapiikihsetawiaanki masaanaapiikwa?” iilikoci kiyošiahi.
en: And then, the old men said to him, “Why did you move the rope on us?”

mya: neehi-hsa: “weenipiilakiaani kati aapoolaapiikihšimaki eehi maaciihkaani masaanaapiikwa!”
en: And (Wiihsakacaakwa) said, “I forgot to put the rope back the same way when I left!”

mya: namehka weecikiimaaci kiyošiahi. kapootwe-hsa, “teepi-nko-hka noohse naawi seekiinaci ceekiši eempahweeciki mahkiikonki?”
en: (Wiihsakacaakwa) lived with the old men a short time. Then, after a while (the old men asked), “Grandson, can’t you go and catch us all kinds of birds out on the lake?”

mya: wiihsakacaakwa neehi-hsa: “taaniši iši-hka sakiinaki?” iilaaci kiyošiahi.
en: Then Wiihsakacaakwa said to the old men, “How am I supposed to catch them?”

mya: “wiihsa wiikapa pihšiinanto. neehi kookiihkani mahkiikonki. neehi wiikapa kihpitoohkani ahkaatawaanki. neehi wiihsa meehci- kihpitooyani ahkaatawaanki, kihpitoohkani kipakwantionenki. neehi pahsaahka mahkiikwi moohkiihkani. ‘ceeki-nko kati aayiihkwe mihtohseeniwiyiikwi oowaaha!’ ilaahkani” iilikoci kiyošiahi wiihsakacaakwa.
en: “Peel a bunch of basswood-bark off the trees. Then you have to dive into the lake. Then tie the basswood-bark to their feet. And after you have tied it to the feet of several of them, you must tie them to your belt. Then you must come to the surface in the middle of the lake. “Then tell them ‘You can’t all live here forever!’” the old men told Wiihsakacaakwa.

mya: neehi-hsa niiši iišilenici kiyošiahi iiši-wiintamaakoci.
en: And so he did as he was told by the old men.

mya: wiihsa ceekiši šiihšiipaki, peehkiihsaki, tapaahsiaki, waapankiaki, ceeki eenswikaateeholaata. eehkwi neešwikaateeholaata ihsa namehka saakikoleehakoki. eehkohkicahakolici. neehi-hsa-hkwa neeneehseeci. neehi-hsa meehci ceeki kiihpilaata pahsaahka
en: All kinds of ducks, brants, Canada geese, swans, he tied their feet all together. Every time he tied two of them together, for a short time he would come up with only his nose out of the water. He floated behind their tails. And then he would take another breath.

mya: moohkiici mahkiikonki. kiyošiahi iišimekoci iišilenici.
en: And after he tied them all, he emerged in the middle of the lake. He did what the old men had told him.

mya: “ceeki-nko kati kiilwa mihtohseeniwiyiikwi waaha!”
en: “You can’t all live here!”(he said).

mya: neehi-hsa ceeki eempahwilici. sakiinaahpa-hka. naahpa-hsa eempahwalikoci. neehi-hsa pilowiši eewalekoci.
en: And then they all flew up. He meant to catch them. Instead, they carried him up. And he was carried far away.

mya: kapootwe-hsa aalaankweeci. “wincamaaci pahkihkaaki wiikapa” iici-hsa.
en: After a while he got tired. “I wish the pieces of bark would break”, said (Wiihsakacaakwa).

mya: neehi-hsa peehkihkaaki. kiihtile paapincinki. eehkwi pimihsaaci, “wiincamaaci kinoonke eehi ahpiihsaani”. neehi-hsa niiyaaha eehpiihsaaci myaalameekwali. peehkihteehkawaaci. neehi-hsa saakaciolaaci siipionkonci. neehi-hsa poohkiciišwaaci. naahpa-hsa mahkooli meehkošwaaci ceenkweepilici.
en: Then they broke. Sure enough, (Wiihsakacaakwa) fell. While he fell (he said) “I hope I land in deep water”. And there he fell on a catfish. He killed it when he landed on it. And he took it out from the river. And then he cut it open. But he cut into a bear sitting inside.

mya: neehi-hsa niiyaaha weeyaahkici teepi ntaahswi kiilhsoohi. sakaanki ceekamaaci mahkooli neehi myaalameekwali.
en: So (Wiihsakacaakwa) lived there several months. Eventually, he ate up the bear and the catfish.

mya: niišwi kiyošiaki keekiipiinkweewaaci neešwiikiwaaci.
en: There were two old blind men living together.

mya: wiihsakacaakwa keewi-mehtohseeniwici. neehi-hsa meehkawaaci kiyošiahi keekiipiinkweelici neešwiikilici. neehi-hsa peentikiici wiikiaaminki. neehi-hsa: “teepi-nko-hka weecikiimilakakoki, nimehšoominka?” aalimiihtoolakoki-hka.”
en: And Wiihsakacaakwa was wandering around, living here and there. And he found the two old blind men living together. Then he entered the house. And then he said: “Can I live with you, my grandfathers? I’ll cook for you.”

mya: neehi-hsa kiyošiaki: “tipeewe-hka iišiteehiaanki wiicikiimiaanke.”
en: So then the old men said: “We’d be glad if you lived with us.”

mya: neehi-hsa teepi ilekahkwi weecikiimaaci. kapootwe hsa, “nakalaayaani” iišiteeheeci, amehšoomahi. neehi hsa weentamawaaci: “aahkwaahkeelintamaani iši-hka wiicikiimilakakoki.” neehi-hka: “aapooši kiiwimehtohsiaani, iišiteehiaani, nimehšoominka”. neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa kweecimolaaci kiyošiahi, “taaniši iši eenkiheekwi ceekiši peemihsaaciki, kiilwa keekiipiinkweeyiikwe?”
en: And then he lived with them for long enough. Soon he decided that he would leave his grandfathers. And then he told them: “I’m getting tired of the way I’m living with you.” And then (he said), “I think I’ll be travelling around again, my grandfathers”. And then Wiihsakacaakwa asked the old men, “how did you kill all those different kinds of birds, you being blind and all?”

mya: kiyošiaki ihsa weentamawaahsiikwi. neehi-hsa kiyošiaki iilaaciki, “aahpitohseeyani-hka. kapootwe-hka aapooši pyaayani. neehi-hka weecikiimiaanki.” neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa maaciihkaaci.
en: The old men wouldn’t tell him. And then the old men said to him: “You can be on your way. You’ll be back again soon enough. Then you’ll live with us.” And then Wiihsakacaakwa left.

mya: neehi-hsa kweehkaapiikihsetawaaci masaanaapiikwali eehiši-hkwa nipi naatiwaaci kiyošiaki. niiši iilaapiikalaaci eehiši iihpahkiiki. neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa neekalaaci kiyošiahi.
en: Then he moved the rope leading to where the old men fetched water. He strung it towards a steep bank. And then Wiihsakacaakwa left the old men.

mya: kapootwe kiyošiaki eeyiihkwiwaaci. neehi-hsa: “aalimiihtootaawi”. neehi-hsa ninkoti: “nipi kati ninaate”. neehi-hsa noontiohseeci, meehkonaaci masaanaapiikaanali. neehi-hsa maaciihkaaci.
en: Soon after, the old men became hungry. And (one of them said): “Let’s cook something”. And one (said): “I’ll fetch some water.” And he went outside, feeling around for the rope. And so he started off.

mya: kapootwe-hsa peelihkanki miiwi. neehi-hsa paapincinki iihpahkionkonci. neehi-hsa weehkamaaci awiihkaanali. neehi-hsa pyaalici.
en: In not too long he stumbled on the path. Then he fell down the hill. Then he called out for his friend. And he came.

mya: “keetwi iilahkiiwiyani, niihka?”
en: “What’s the matter with you, my friend?”

mya: “paapincinaani. weekiwi nahohseelo. naapiši-hka kipaapincine.”
en: “I fell down! Be careful how you walk! You might fall down too!”

mya: neehi-hsa ninkoti niilaahkawaaci masaanaapiikwali. neehi hsa meehkonaaci masaanaapiikwaali. neehi-hsa eetaahpahaaci awiihkaanali. neehi-hsa saakaciweeci. neehi-hsa: “koohsemina kweehkaapiikihsetoolankwa masaanaapiikwali.” neehi-hsa aapwe peentikiiwaaci wiikiaaminki.
en: And so he threw him a rope. And he felt around for the rope. And he pulled his friend out. And then he emerged on top of the bank. And then he said: “Our grandchild changed the ropes on us!” And then they went back into the house.

mya: “taaniši-hka ihpenalankwi koohsemina?”
en: “What shall we do to our grandchild?”

mya: “eetaahpiswankwi.”
en: “We should draw him by smoke”.

mya: neehi-hsa moohkinalaawaaci ahpwaakanali. neehi-hsa eehpwaawaaci. eetaahpiswaawaaci wiihsakacaakwali.
en: And then they filled up the pipe. And then they smoked. They drew Wiihsakacaakwa by smoking.

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa aapwe pyaaci. ahkwaanteemi paahkihsenki. neehi-hsa kiimi peentikiici.
en: And then Wiihsakacaakwa came back. The door opened. Then he snuck in.

mya: neehi-hsa ninkoti kiyošia: “leni naahpa meelaawaki koohsemina wiihsakacaakwa”. neehi-hsa kiyošiaki: “ahkwaanteemi kipwihsaace”, iišiteeheewaaci. kiipwaahsinki.
en: And then one of the old men said: “It seems as though I smell our grandchild Wiihsakacaakwa”. And then the old men thought: “Let the door close”. The wind blew it shut.

mya: kiyošiaki: “ankihaahkaawi wiihsakacaakwa”. neehi-hsa ahcikiwa naaninkoti eeyoowaaci neenatwahwaawaaci. meehci kiipahwaawaaci, neehi-hsa neenatwahwaawaaci.
en: The old men (said): “We should kill Wiihsakacaakwa”. And then, using some fish-spears, they began taking turns jabbing around for him. After they shut him in they jabbed around for him.

mya: kapootwe-hsa wiihsakacaakwa aalaankweeci. neehi-hsa aacimwiihtawaaci, “nimehšoominka, ankihihsooko.”
en: Soon Wiihsakacaakwa got tired. And then he spoke to them, “My grandfathers, don’t kill me!”

mya: neehi-hsa: “kiila-nko, wiihsakacaakwe?”
en: (Then the old men said), “is that you, Wiihsakacaakwa?”

mya: “niila, nimehšoominka. aapwe pyaayaani. aapooši-hka aalimiihtoolakoki ankihihsiiweekwe”.
en: “It’s me, my grandfathers. I’ve come back. I’ll cook for you again if you don’t kill me”.

mya: neehi-hsa kiyošiaki: “kiila-nko kweehkaapiikihsetawiaanki masaanaapiikwa, eehiši-hkwa nipi naatiaanki?”
en: And then the old men (said): “Were you the one who moved the guide-rope on us, to where we used to fetch water?”

mya: “kiihtilaami niila kweehkaapiikihšimaka masaanaapiikwa, neehi weenipiilakiaani kati aapweepiikihšimaka eehkwi maaciihkaani. inko alehši iihpinalilakoki”.
en: “Indeed I was the one who moved the ropes, then I forgot to change them back while I was leaving. I didn’t do it to you on purpose.”

mya: neehi-hsa kiyošiaki: “aapooši-hka weecikiimiaanki”.
en: And then the old men said: “You can live with us again.”

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa weecikiimaaci teepi ilekahkwi. kapootwe-hsa wiihsakacaakwa aahkwaahkiilintanki iiši wiicikiimaaci kiyošiahi. neehi-hsa: “ancaamaci wiintamawiyiikwi iiši-sakiineekwi peehkiihsaki, šiihšiipaki.”
en: And then Wiihsakacaakwa lived with them for long enough. Soon, Wiihsakacaakwa got tired of the way he was living with the old men. And then (he said): “I wish you’d tell me how you catch those ducks and geese.”

mya: “moohci aalimahsiinoowi iiši-sakiininci. kapootwe-hka nipihsinkiši ayaayani, niiyaaha wiihsa neewaci ceekiši keeyohsaaciki. neehi-hka wiihsa masaanaapiikoonsaki eewalaci. neehi-hka ceeki kiihpilaci kipakwantionenki. neehi-hka napaliahkonci nipihsinki kookiiyani. neehi-hka ahkaatiwa kiihpilahwaci”.
en: “It’s not difficult to catch them. Sometime when you go to the lake, right there you’ll see all kinds of them flying around. Then, you take several small pieces of twine. And you tie them all onto your belt. Then, you dive in on one side of the lake. And then you tie their feet.”

mya: kapootwe-hsa-hkwa saakikoleehakoci. neehi-hsa-hkwa neeneehseeci. aapwe kookiici. aapooši kiihpitawaaci ahkaata.
en: Every now and then he would stick his nose out of the water while he was floating. Then he would take more breaths. And he dove back. Again he tied their feet.

mya: neehi-hsa meehci wiihsa kiihpilaaci moohkiici pahsaahkaha nipihsinki. neehi-hsa: “inko-hka moošaki meehtohseeniwiyiikwi oowaaha”. neehi-hsa ceeki eempahowaaci. iši-hka sakiinaahpa iišimekoci kiyošiahi. naahpa-hsa eewalekoci eempahwilici peminki.
en: And after he tied several of them, he emerged in the middle of the lake. And then he said: “You can’t always live here”. And then they all flew up. He was going to catch them that way, like he was told by the old men. Instead, he was lifted into the air when they flew up.

mya: keeyawalikoci teepi ilekahkwi. kapootwe aalaankweeci iši keeyawalinci.
en: They carried him around long enough. Soon he got tired from the way he was being carried around.

mya: neehi-hsa: “ancaamaci kihpitaakana pahkihkaaka”. neehi-hsa peehkihkaaki. neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa paapincinki.
en: And then he thought: “I wish the strings would break”. And then they broke. And then Wiihsakacaakwa fell.

mya: teepi ilekahkwi kwaantihsaaci. kapootwe-hsa ahpwaayoni iišiteeheeci. neehi-hsa moohkinalaaci ahpwaakanali. neehi-hsa eehpwaaci eehkwi kwaantihsaaci. neehi-hsa-hkwa aapwalaapici aahkole neekatanki. “inko-hka naapi iišilenici aweeya. niilaahka teehši niiši iišileniaani”.
en: He plummeted for some time. After a while he decided to smoke. And so he filled up a pipe. And so he smoked while he fell. And then he looked back at the smoke he had left behind. “No one else can do that. I’m the only one who can do that”.

mya: neehi-hsa kapootwe kiikoo neenki mahtahkiši. neehi-hsa: “taanaaha toki kati ahpiihsaani. ancaamaci eehi kinoonki nipi eehpiihsaani”. neehi-hsa: “kweehtamaani naahpa-hka eehkalaamwiaani”. neehi-hsa aapooši, “ancaamaci waalahkionki kaakipakwaki moohkineewaaci”.
en: And soon after he saw something down below. And (he said): “I wonder where I’ll land? I hope I land in deep water”. And then: “I’m afraid I might drown.” And again, “I wish for a hollow filled with leaves!”

mya: neehi-hsa šaaye ciikaahkwe piihsaaci. neehi-hsa peehtweeci. “ancaamaci waalahkionki ahpiihsaani”, iihpa-hka. “naahpa tawaaninki piintikiihsaani”, iici-hsa. neehi-hsa peentikiihsaaci poohkancionki tawaaninki.
en: By now he was already coming up close. Then he said the wrong thing. “I wish I’d fall into a hollow”, he said. “But I’m falling into a tree!” he said. And he fell into a hollow tree.

mya: neehi-hsa “taaniši-hka iiši-noontiohsiaani?” iišintanki awiiyawi. neehi-hsa kweekweeteelici iši-hka noontiohseeci. neehi-hsa aalweelici.
en: And then he said: “How can I get out of here?” And then he kept trying to get out. And he couldn’t.

mya: kapootwe-hsa aweeyahi noontawaaci aayaacimolici. neehi hsa ciikaahkwe pyaalici noontaahkwahamoowaaci tawaani. neehi-hsa mitemohsaki noontawaawaaci mahkooli. neehi-hsa poohkahamoowaaci tawaani. neehi-hsa wiihsakacaakwa niiyaaha amiihsokiaakanahi saakihšimaaci eehi poohkahki.
en: Soon he heard some people talking. And then as they came close, he started knocking at the tree. And these women heard him as a bear. So they cut a hole in the tree. And Wiihsakacaakwa’s pubic hairs were sticking out there through the hole.

mya: neehi-hsa mitemohsaki aapweeyaawaaci eehiši kihkihšiwaaci. neehi-hsa weentamawaawaaci aleniahi, “meehkawakinci mahkwa tawaaninki”.
en: So the women went back to where they were camping. And they told the men, “We found a bear in a tree”.

mya: neehi-hsa aleniaki: “nawi ankihaataawi”, iilitiiwaaci.
en: And then the men said to each other: “Let’s go kill him”.

mya: neehi-hsa niiši iiyaawaaci tawaani. meehkamoowaaci, keewahamoowaaci ihsa-hka. neehi-hsa meehcaalakahamoowaaci. neehi-hsa seekihenci wiihsakacaakwa. neehi-hsa keelolaaci, “ankihihsooko, niihkaaninka.”
en: And then they went toward the tree. They found it, and were going to cut it down. And so they cut the hole bigger. And then Wiihsakacaakwa was frightened. And then he spoke to them: “Don’t kill me, my friends!”

mya: neehi-hsa noontiohseeci. neehi-hsa: “wiici mehtohseeniyomelakoki.”
en: And then (Wiihsakacaakwa) stepped out. And then (he said): “I want to be a human with you!”

mya: mahweewa ihsa peempaalici ciikaahkwi siipionki. neehi-hsa aašitehkawaaci ahšiimali paapankamwali.
en: Wolf was walking along near a river. And then he came across his little brother fox.

mya: neehi-hsa: “taanonci pyaayani, nihšiime?”
en: (Wolf said) “Where are you coming from, brother?”

mya: neehi-hsa paapankamwa, “oowaanci siipionkonci pyaayaani”.
en: Fox (replied), “I’m coming from the river, over yonder.”

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa, “keetwi meeciyani weecihsaamilaani paapankamwe? noohkwaantamani kitooni, kiikoo meeciyani weenkanki.”
en: Then wolf (said): “What have you been eating, brother fox? You’re licking your mouth, you’ve been eating something good.”

mya: neehi-hsa paapankamwa, “weecihsaamilaani mahweewe, aamaawia paankosaakani meeciaani.”
en: Fox (replied), “Brother wolf, I’ve been eating honey.”

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa: “taanaaha eehteeki paankosaakani weecihsaamilaani paapankamwe? niiši awaašilo! naapiši weenkitamaani aamaawia paankosaakani. naawe-miicitaawi weecihsaamilaani paapankamwe.”
en: And then wolf (said): “Where is the honey located, brother fox? Take me there! I want to eat some honey too. Let’s go and eat some, brother fox.”

mya: “niiši-hka eewalelaani weecihsaamilaani”. neehi-hsa paapankamwa eewalaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali.
en: (Fox replied,) “I’ll take you over there, brother.” So then fox led his brother wolf (there).

mya: neehi-hsa meehkawaawaaci waapiihkiciahi ašihseewa. neehi-hsa weecihsaamaacili paapankamwali, “ooniini eehi ahteeki aamaawia paankosaakani, weecihsaamilaani mahweewe. pinahamani-hka ašihsayi, niiyaaha eehteeki wiihsa aamaawia paankosaakani. weecihsaamilaani mahweewe, inko-hka teepi weeciilamelaani. maalami wiihsa meeciaani aamaawia paankosaakani. ahpiihtohsiaani-hka weecihsaamilaani mahweewe. kiilaahka peenahamani ašihsayi. neehi-hka kiilaahka ceeki meeciyani aamaawia paankosaakani”.
en: Then they found the bumble bees’ nest. And then fox (said) to his brother, “Here’s where the honey is, brother wolf. If you knock the nest off, there’s a lot of honey there. I have not helped you enough, brother wolf. I’ve already eaten too much honey. I’ll be moving on, brother wolf. You should knock off the nest by yourself. Then you can have the honey all to yourself.”

mya: neehi-hsa paapankamwa neekalaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali. aacimwi-hsa neekalaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali.
en: And then fox left his brother wolf. He pretended to leave his brother wolf.

mya: neehi-hsa paapankamwa aapwe pyaaci. ciikaahkwe keemaapamaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali. neehi-hsa mahweewa eempihsaaci pinahanki ašihsayi. noolihsaaci. aapooši kweeteelici. pilwiši iiyaaci. neehi-hsa meemikwiici eempihsaaci. neehi-hsa peenahanki ašihsayi. neehi-hsa waapiihkiciahi poohkahanki ašihseewa. neehi-hsa waapiihkiciahi šeehšahakoci misaahaki antepikani. neehi-hsa paahkiinkweeci. aayaahkami keekiipiinkweeci.
en: And then fox came back. From up close he spied on his brother wolf. Wolf was jumping up, trying to knock down the nest. He couldn’t jump high enough. He tried again. He went off a ways. Then he ran back and jumped. And he knocked down the nest. He broke open the bumble bees’ nest. The bumble bees stung him all over his head. His face swelled up. He went totally blind.

mya: neehi-hsa weecihsaamaacili paapankamwali keeweešinaakoci. neehi-hsa paapankamwa neekalaaci weecihsaamaacili. meehci wanimaaci mahweewali, pilwiši ihsa iiyaaci. kiihkeelintanki weecihsaamaacili mahweewali ihsa-hka ahtimikoci. neehi-hsa pilwi eehpyaaci. keehkiiweelici. “inko-hka meehkawici weecihsaamaka mahweewa!”
en: Then his brother fox laughed at him. And then fox left his brother. After he had tricked wolf, he went far away. He knew that his brother wolf would try to catch up with him. He went far away. He laughed and laughed. “My brother wolf won’t find me!”

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa peelakiici meehci waapiihkiciahi šeehšahakoci. neehi-hsa mahweewa aapooši-hsa: “weecihsaamaka paapankamwa weenimici. aalime-hka ahtemaka weecihsaamaka paapankamwa. maamihšihka kati ankihaka iiši-wanimici.”
en: And then wolf recovered after the bumble bees stung him. And wolf (said) again: “My brother fox tricked me. I’m bound to catch up with brother fox. If I get near him, I’ll kill him for tricking me like that.”

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa maaciihkaaci. meehkanki eehi peemihkaweelici weecihsaamaacili paapankamwali. neehi hsa mahweewa: “aalime-hka ahtemaka weecihsaamaka paapankamwa.” neehi-hsa eehtimaaci paapankamwali.
en: And then wolf set off. He found where his brother fox had left some footprints. And then wolf (said): “I’m bound to catch up with brother fox”. And so he caught up with fox.

mya: neewaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali ciikaahkwe pyaalici. neehi-hsa paapankamwa meemikwiihsaaci. neehi-hsa ciikaahkwe pyaaci mahweewa. neehi-hsa paapankamwa seekihenci. “inko hka nawanswaki”, iišiteeheeci paapankamwa. neehi-hsa weelantaweehsaaci tawaaninki eehciyohkaapawiki siipionkiši. “aapooši kati wanimaka weecihsaamaka mahweewa”.
en: (Fox) saw his brother wolf coming near. And then fox ran off. And wolf came near. And fox got scared. “I can’t outrun him”, fox thought. And so (fox) quickly climbed up a tree leaning towards the river. “I’m going to trick brother wolf again”.

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa neehpyaaci tawaaninki. kweelihkaweewaaci. “taaniši toki ayaaci weecihsaamaka paapankamwa?”  keewaahtoohseeci-hsa tawaaninki. neewaahsiikwi tawaaninki  ceenkweepilici. neehi-hsa neewaaci weecihsaamaacili  paapankamwali acihciikamali nipinki. mahweewa iilaaci-hsa:  “aalime-kati ankihilaani, weecihsaamilaani paapankamwe!”
en: And then wolf got to the tree. He lost his trail. “I wonder which way my brother fox went?” He went around the tree. He didn’t see  (fox) sitting in the tree. And then he saw his brother fox’s reflection  in the water. Wolf said to him, “I’m bound to kill you, brother  fox!”

mya: neehi-hsa paapankamwa keeweeliinkweeci. waapamaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali.
en: And fox was grinning. He was looking at his brother wolf.

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa ceešiikiteeci. “aalime kati weecihsaamilaani paapankamwe sakiinilaani!” neehi-hsa mahweewa ceemonkihsaaci nipinki. kookiici. neehi-hsa saakaciiweeci. aapwalaapici-hsa nipinki. aapooši neewaaci weecihsaamaacili keeweeliinkweeta paapankamwa. neehi-hsa mahweewa: “aalime-kati weecihsaamilaani sakiinilaani”, iilaaci-hsa.
en: Then wolf got angry. “I’m bound to catch you, brother fox!” And then wolf jumped into the water. He dove. And then he crawled out. He looked back in the water. Again he saw his brother fox grinning. And then wolf said: “I’m bound to catch you, brother!”

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa ahsenali kiihpilaaci ahkweekaninki, iši kati kookiici sakiinaaci weecihsaamaacili paapankamwali. neehi-hsa ceemonkihsaaci nipinki. neehi-hsa kookiici. neehi-hsa aalweelici kati moohkiici. maalami keehcakolici ihsa ahsenali. neehi-hsa eehkalaamwita toki awiiyawi.
en: And then wolf tied a stone to his neck, so that he could dive and catch his brother fox. And then he jumped into the water. And then he dove. And he failed to come up. The stone was too heavy. And then he drowned himself.

mya: neehi-hsa weecihsaamaacili paapankamwali keehkiiwešinaakota. neehi-hsa paapankamwa kwaantici tawaaninkonci, meehci eenkihaaci weecihsaamaacili mahweewali. “inko-hka noonki eenkihici weecihsaamaka mahweewa”.
en: And brother fox laughed at him. And fox came down from the tree, after he had killed his brother wolf. “Brother wolf won’t kill me now!”

mya: paapankamwa ihsa peempaalici aašoohkooninki kiihkoneehsahi eewalaaci. neehi-hsa: “niwanimaa-hka nihseensa mahweewa”, iišintanka awiiyawi paapankamwa. neehi-hsa aahpitohseeci eelaakwiki. neepanki-hsa. kiihtile aašitehkawaaci ahseensali mahweewali.
en: Fox was walking along the ice carrying some fish. Then: “I’m going to fool my older brother wolf”, fox said to himself. And then he travelled on into the evening. It was very cold. Sure enough, he met his older brother wolf.

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa: “taanonci piilaci kiihkoneehsaki, nihšiime paapankamwe?”
en: And then wolf said: “Where did you get those fish, brother fox?”

mya: “siipionki seekiinakiki”.
en: “I caught them at the river.”

mya: “taaniši iši seekiinaci?”
en: “How did you catch them?”

mya: “wiihsa moohci aalimahsiinoowi iši-seekiininci kiihkoneehsaki. eewalelaani-hka eehi sakiinaki wiihsa kiihkoneehsaki.”
en: “It’s not hard to catch a lot of fish. I’ll take you to where I catch all these fish.”

mya: neehi-hsa neešohkawaaci. neehi-hsa meehkamoowaaci eehi meehtoohseeniaki poohkahamoowaaci aašoohkooni, eehonci nipi eewatoowaaci. paapankamwa: “oowaaha wiihsa seekiinakiki kiihkoneehsaki. noonki kati wiintamoolaani iiši-sakiininci kiihkoneehsaki. niiyaaha-hka ceemonkisihtooyani kinsooyi. neehi-hka waapanwi niiyaaha ceenkweepiyani aašoohkooninki. neehi-hka šayiipaawe eetaahpahtooyani kinsooyi. neehi-hka kiihkoneehsaki eekoosiciki kinsooyinki.”
en: And then the two of them went off together. And then they found a place where some humans had cut a hole in the ice, where they carried water. Fox (said): “Right here I catch a lot of fish. Now I’ll tell you how one catches fish. You put your tail in the water there. And then you sit there on the ice all night long. And then, in the morning you pull your tail out. There’ll be fish hanging from your tail.

mya: meehci weentamawaaci paapankamwa ahseensali mahweewali iši kati sakiinaalici kiihkoneehsahi. neehi-hsa: “nihseense mahweewe noonki kati nakalilaani. maalami neepanki. maacaani kati.” neehi hsa paapankamwa keehkiiweešinawaaci ahseensali mahweewali. neehi-hsa weecihsaaminta paapankamwa neekalaaci ahseensali mahweewali. neehi-hsa mahweewa wiilaahka neekalenci.
en: After fox told his brother wolf how to catch fish, he then (said): “Brother wolf, I’ll leave you now. It’s too cold. I’m going home.” Then fox laughed at his brother wolf. Then brother fox left his brother wolf. Then wolf was left alone.

mya: neehi-hsa ceemonkisihtooki ansooyi. “taanaaha toki eentaahswi sakiinaki kiihkoneehsaki šayiipawe?” iišintanki awiiyawi. neehi hsa niiyaaha ceenkweepici waapanwi. neehi-hsa aašoohkooni kiipwatenki. neehi-hsa ansooyi soonkatenki aašoohkooninki. neehi-hsa aalweelici kati eetaahpahtooki ansooyi.
en: And then (wolf) stuck his tail in the water. “I wonder how many fish I’ll catch by morning?” he said to himself. And so he sat there til dawn. And the ice froze solid. And his tail froze in the ice. And he couldn’t pull his tail out.

mya: “maalami piici wiihsa seekiinaki kiihkoneehsaki. iini wiiyoonkonci aalweeliaani kati pasekwiaani.”
en: “I must have caught too many fish. That’s why I can’t get up.”

mya: neehi-hsa maamihšihka peehkihtiaacici. “ancaamaci aweeya pyaaci iši-hka poohkahamawici nisooyi.”
en: And he was just about to freeze to death. “I wish someone would come to poke a hole (in the ice) for my tail.”

mya: neehi-hsa meehtohseenia nipi naatiki pyaaci. neehi-hsa meehkawaaci mahweewali ansooyi soonkatenki aašoohkooninki.
en: Just then a human came along to fetch some water. And he found wolf with his tail frozen into the ice.

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewa: “ankihihsoolo!”, iilaaci meehtoohseeniali. neehi-hsa aapooši: “poohkahamawilo aahšoohkooni.”
en: And wolf said to the human: “Don’t kill me!” Then, again, he said “Cut a hole in the ice!”

mya: neehi-hsa poohkahamoonci. neehi-hsa eehtaahpahtooki ansooyi. meeneehwiciki kiihkoneehsaki. “aapooši weenimita nihšiima paapankamwa! aalime-hka miihkohkawaka kapootwe. taaniši hkwe ihpenalaki. inko-hka noonki eentoneehwaki nihšiima paapankamwa.”
en: And then a hole was made for him. And he pulled his tail out. There were no fish. “My little brother fox has tricked me again! I’m bound to meet up with him eventually. I don’t know what I’ll do with him. I’m not going to go after my little brother fox now.”

mya: eehsipana ihsa peempaalici ciikaahkwe siipionki. eentoneehwaaci saahkiahi, iši kati amwaaci.
en: Raccoon was traveling along near a river. He was hunting for crawfishes to eat.

mya: neehi-hsa meehkanki eehi siipiiwi kwaantihtanki. niiyaaha-hsa kiinoonki nipi.
en: Then he found a place where the river had falls. The water was deep there.

mya: neehi-hsa wiihsa neewaaci saahkiahi eehi kinoonki. “taaniši toki hka iši-wanimaki saahkiaki, iši-hka saakaciweewaaci, iši-hka sakiinaki neehi-hka eemwakiki? neehi-hsa eehsipana: “aacimwi kati nipeyaani ciikaahkwe eehi siipiiwi kwaantihtanki”.
en: And then he saw a lot of crawfishes where it was deep. “How on earth can I trick the crawfishes into crawling out of the water, so I can catch them and eat them?” And then raccoon (thought): “I’ll pretend to be dead, near where the waterfall is.”

mya: neehi-hsa niiyaaha ciikaahkwe nipinki taahtakiihšinki aacimwi neepiki. neehi-hsa saahkiaki aalinta saakaciweewaaci. neehi-hsa neewaawaaci eehsipanali. “kiihtilaami toki neepiki kihseensina”, iilitiiwaaci saahkiaki.
en: So then he laid down there near the water, pretending to be dead. And then some of the crawfishes crawled out (of the water). And then they saw raccoon. “It sure looks like our brother is dead”, the crawfishes said to each other.

mya: neehi-hsa aalinta kweehsaawaaci. “aacimwi piici neepika kihseensina”.
en: But some of them were still afraid of him. “I think our elder brother is pretending to be dead”.

mya: neehi-hsa, “niilaahka kiimi seehsinaka aciitinki, iši-hka amatinaki aacimwi neepiki. kiihtilaami nipeke, inko-hka toohkiici. neehi-hka nipeke, neemikaayankwi kiiwaahci eehi‑taahtakiihšinki.”
en: And then, (one said), ‘I’ll sneak up by myself and pinch him on his anus, so that I’ll wake him up if he’s pretending to be dead. If he’s really dead, he won’t move. And if he is dead, we’ll have a dance around where he’s lying down.”

mya: kiihtile wiihsa saahkiaki saakaciweewaaci. neehi-hsa neemikaawaaci kiiwaahci eehsipanali. neehi-hsa eehsipana kiilawi peesikwiihsaaci. neehi-hsa wiihsa eenkihaaci saahkiahi. eemwaaci. aalinta saahkiaki ceemonkihsaawaaci nipinkiši.
en: Sure enough, a bunch of crawfish emerged from the water. Then they danced around the raccoon. Then suddenly raccoon jumped to his feet. And then he killed a bunch of the crawfishes. He ate them. Some of the crawfishes jumped into the water.

mya: noohsa iiši-wiintinci ‘ciinkwaahkia’. neeyakosici awansapiicalakonci meehšaaki siipiiwi. mayaawi neepihkia, wiihsa peelakiihaata mihtohseeniahi eehkwi mihtohseenwici.
en: My father was called ‘Ciinkwaahkia’. He was born on the east side of Big River. He was a great doctor, he cured many people during his life.

mya: iihpisita, meehcikilita, meenkiteliweeta, tikawi waapikilookiita. pahsaahkaha eepihkiita awiilhsa. moohswaya mahkisinaakana peesihkanka, eetaahsita moošaki. namehka weehkweetiita eehkwi nipehsiikwi.
en: He was tall, big-bodied, broad-shouldered, and a little light skinned. He had braids in the middle of his hair. He wore buckskin moccasins, and he always wore leggings. For a short time before he died he wore trousers.

mya: nkotenwi akima peewaaliahi waayaahtaanwa siipionki neehi kiišiwa siipionki. meehci aancihseenki tahkinka-siipionki niišwi pipoonwi meehtohseenwita, neehi neepika. awiiwali mahtami neepikili. neekalaata nihswi piloohsahi.
en: Once he was the chief of the Peoria at Wea River and Bull River. After moving to Spring River, he lived for two years, then he died. His wife had died first. He left three children.

mya: koohsina peehkahkionkiši weeyaahkiyani kiwiinsoonemi meehceelintaminki.
en: Our father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

mya: ancamaaci akimaayoni pyaace iišileniyani ašiihkionki naapi iišinaakwahki peehkahkionkiši.
en: Give us this day our daily bread.

mya: miililoome kaahkiihkwe miicioni eekami waapanki. neehi pooneelintanto mahsenahamaanki.
en: And forgive us our debts

mya: naapiši pooneelintamawakinci ansaahki mahsenahaminki.
en: As we forgive what others owe us

mya: aapooši meeleewahkionkonci awašihsooloome neehi nahawašiloome.
en: Also lead us not into evil, but deliver us into righteousness

mya: wiiyoonkonci kitakimaayoni, kiila šiinšiilawiyani, kiila peehkiilintamani, moošaki aayaahkami. amen.
en: For thine is the kindgom, and the power, and the glory forever. Amen.

mya: mihtami myaamiaki nipinkonci saakaciweeciki. eehonci saakaci weewaaci ‘saakiiweeyonki’ iitamenki.
en: At first the Myaamia came out of the water. The place they emerged is called ‘Coming Out Place’.

mya: nipinkonci neeweeyohsaaciki moohkiiciki. “peemitanaahkwahki sakaahkweelo”, iilitiiciki.
en: The first ones emerged from the water. “Grab ahold of tree limbs” they told each other.

mya: neehi saakaciweeciki. noonki niiyaahi eeminooteeciki. niiyaanci maaciihkaaciki. minooteeni neekatankiki.
en: And they came out. Then they formed a town there. From there they went away. They left the town.

mya: kapootwe nkoti aapweeyaata. aapwe pyaata kwitakaki mihtohseeniaki neewaaciki saakiiweeyonki. naahpa-hsa naapi iilaataweeciki iilataaweeyaanki. neehi-hsa weentaawaaci. ‘matehkohkisenaakana’ iilaaciki iina mihtohseeniaki. moohci ninkihkeelimaahsoo weencinaakosiwaaci. moohci aweeyaki kihkeelimaawaata eehi ayaawaaci.
en: After a while one returned. When he came back he saw the other people at Coming Out Place. To our surprise, their language was just like our language. They gave them a name. ‘Old Moccasins’ he called those people. I don’t know where they were from. Nobody knew where they went.

mya: ooniini ninkiiki iišimiwaaci, ninkya seekaahkweeta amihsali waapankihkwa. ceeki mihtohseeniaki kiyošiaki eelaamihtankiki.
en: This is how my mothers told me, my mother Seekaahkweeta, and her older sister Waapankihkwa. All the old Indian men believed it.

mya: siipiiwi ‘saakiiweesiipiiwi’ weentankiki, eehonci saakaciweewaaci. iiniini wiiyoonkonci niiši weentinciki ‘seekaahkweeta’, ‘seekaahkonanka’, ‘seekaahkohkwa’.
en: They call the river ‘Coming Out River’ at the place where they came out from. Because of this people are named ‘Seekaahkweeta’, ‘Seekaahkonanka’, and ‘Seekaahkohkwa’.

mya: nkoti peehkonteeki waapanswa mahkwa aalimweetaatiiciki.
en: One night rabbit and bear were quarreling with each other.

mya: mahkwa: “tipeewe-hka moošaki peehkonteeki. peemaka nimehkaakooki mihtohseeniaki.”
en: Bear (said), “It would be good if it was always dark. Humans would never find me.”

mya: waapanswa: “tipeewe-hka moošaki waahseehkiki” iilaata mahkooli, “nišihsaki kiinaakwi meehkoohkiki eenkihehkiki.”
en: Rabbit said to bear, “It would be good if it was always daylight, so that my uncles could find you and kill you”.

mya: neehi mahkwa: “miihkintiitaawi”, iilaata waapansooli. “niila kati ‘peehkonteece’ niiši nintelwee. kiila kati ‘waapance’ niiši kitelwee. anehilaane pihkonteewi kati. anehiyane waahseewi kati.”
en: Bear then said to rabbit, “Let’s make a bet. I’ll say ‘Let it be dark’. You’ll say ‘Let it be light’. If I beat you, it will be dark. If you beat me it will be light”.

mya: neehi weehšiyohkaatiiciki. mahkwa iilweeci: “pihkonteece, pihkonteece, pihkonteece”.
en: And so they started on each other. bear said “let it be dark, let it be dark, let it be dark”.

mya: waapanswa iilweeci: “waapance, waapance, waapance.”
en: Rabbit said “let it be light, let it be light, let it be light”.

mya: namahkahkike naahpa waahseeki. mahkwa ceešikiteeta. “kitanihi!” iilaata. seehsiinkweenaata, atooni peminkonci peehsinanka. taawitoneenaata.
en: In a little while, it became light. Bear became angry. “You beat me!” he said. He scratched his face, and split his upper lip. He made him hare-lipped.

mya: iiniini wiiyoonkonci moošaki waahseeki. iiniini wiiyoonkonci waapanswa taawitonki.
en: That’s why it’s always light. That’s why rabbits are hare-lipped.

mya: iilweeciki mitemhsa eencihkwita “wiihkata waapanswa antepikani miicihsoolo”, taawitonka kati aniicaanhsali.
en: They would tell a pregnant woman, “You don’t ever eat a rabbit’s head”, (or else) her child would be hare-lipped.

mya: paapankamwa peempaalita kiimoteta pimi. meehci kiimoteta miihsitonaakani meehkaayonaata.
en: Once fox was walking along (when) he stole some grease. After he stole it, he greased his whiskers.

mya: neehi-hsa mahweewali aašitehkawaata. “keetwi iihši meeciyani? meehkaawitonani.”
en: Then he ran into wolf. “What have you been eating, little brother? Your mouth is all greasy.”

mya: neehi-hsa: “alikonci eekotenki. kiila iihpisiyani. teepi teepihsaayani.”
en: Then he replied: “It’s hanging over there. You’re tall enough, you can reach it.”

mya: “pimi niiyaašilo, iihši.”
en: “Take me to this grease, little brother.”

mya: “ooniini eekotenki pimi oowaaha”, iilaata ahseensali mahweewa.
en: “The grease is hanging right here”, (fox) said to his older brother wolf.

mya: neehi mahweewa eempihsaata. poohkantanka ašihsayi waawaapiihkiciaki. neehi šeehšahakota misaahaki antepikaninki.
en: Then wolf jumped up. He bit a hole in the hornets’ nest. And they stung (wolf) all over his head.

mya: meehci aamaawia waawaapiihkiciaki šeehšahaakota mahweewa ceešikiteeta. “noonki iihši kitankihele kati!”, iilaata. paapankamwa maacaamwita.
en: After the hornets stung him all over, wolf became angry. “Now I’m going to kill you, brother!”, he said to him. Fox ran off.

mya: noonki mahweewa keeleešiwaata. paapankamwa eehkwamaahkweeta tawaani šišwici siipiiwi. mahweewa neewaata nipinki. “noonki kinepe, iihši!”
en: Then wolf went after him. Then fox climbed up a tree along the river’s edge. Wolf saw him in the water. “Now you will die, little brother!”

mya: noonki eempihsaata mahweewa nipinki. seehsiihsantanka nipi. saakaciweeta. eehkwa neewaata ahšiimali nipinki keeweešinaakota. ayoolhka ceešikiteeta. “noonki kisakiinile!” iilaata.
en: Then wolf jumped into the water. He bit at the water over and over again. He got out. He still saw his younger brother in the water laughing at him. He got even angrier. “Now I’ll get you!” he said.

mya: noonki tawaani peehšaahkinanka alakiihkwi. ahkweekanenki ahseni kiihpitooka. noonki nipinki eempihsaata. eehkalaamwita.
en: He then peeled some bark off a tree. He tied a stone to his neck. He then jumped into the water and drowned.

mya: eehinki eehkwaapiikaasita.
en: That’s as far as he goes.

mya: teekwaakia iilweeci kiinoonki neemacihsinwi siipionki, niiyaahi niiwi mile peoria wintenonkiši, wintenonki neehpikanki atahkohkani. meehtohseeniaki weentankiki “aašipehkwa weeweencihkwapici”.
en: Teekwaakia (Captain Brouillette) told about a deep spot in the Mississinewa river, about four miles up the river from Peoria, upriver from the red bridge. The people call it “stone cliffs facing each other”.

mya: manetoowa weeyaahkita iilweeciki. ‘lenipinšia’ iilaaciki.
en: A manitou lives there, they say. They call him ‘lenipinšia’.

mya: ahseema meehtohkišwaaciki ceemonkaahkiiciki. kiikoo neetotamawaaciki neetaweelintamoowaaci.
en: They would cut up tobacco and throw it in the water. They would ask him for things they wanted.

mya: teekwaakia neepaasawita. awiiwali peemihsahikota. neehpyaaci ahseemaali peehkišwaata. ceemonkaahkiita. ayaapia, niišwi myaalameekwaki neetotamawaata. awiiwali: “ntotamawi peepanšiinkwia” iilikota.
en: Teekwaakia was out night hunting. His wife was rowing him (in the boat). When he got there, he cut off a piece of tobacco. He threw it in the water. He asked for a buck and two catfish. His wife said to him: “Ask for a white perch”.

mya: wintenonkiši eehi waakihsenki meehcikilita ayaapia eenkihaata. noonki aapweeyaaciki naaminoonkiši. iihkoonki eehpyaaciki. myaalameekwaki aašitehkawaaciki. mihšiiliwaki, wiihsa. noonki ciikiwi peekamaata. nkoti eenkihaata. poosaahkiita. niišanwi peekamaata. niišwi eenkihaata. noonki peekamiiki. moohci neewaawaata noohki.
en: Upstream, where there was a bend (in the river), he killed a big buck. Then they went back downstream. They came to a place where it was shallow. They met up with some catfish. There were a lot of them, a whole bunch. Then he hit one with a fish gig. He killed one. He threw it in the boat. He struck two more times and killed two more. Now the water was muddy. They couldn’t see them anymore.

mya: naaminoonkiši neehpyaaciki eehi kinoonki. niiyaaha šišwici neepawita peepanšiinkwia. noonki peekamaata ciikiwi. eewatookota eehi kinoononkiši. awiiwali iilaata: “ciikiwi”. naatika seekiinanka. eehkwa niiyaaha kiihkoneehsa weeyaahkiita. “noonki ahšakiciihanto!” iilaata. “noonki aapwalahanto!” iilaata.
en: Now they arrived at a place downstream where it was deep. There by the water’s edge stood a white perch. Then he struck with the fish gig. He took him into where it was deep. To his wife, he said “the spear!” He went for it and got hold of it. Still, the fish stayed right there. “Now push it back!” he said to her. “Now back it!” he said to her.

mya: “seekisiaani kinoononkiši iiyaaki mihsooli.” ninciikiaahkomi weecilamaka. eehšakiciihamaani eehiši ihkoonki.
en: “I’m afraid the boat will go into the deep water.” With my gigging pole I helped her. I shoved it back to where it was shallow.

mya: kapootwe ninciikiaahkomi leni aweeya seekiinamawita. seekisiaani ayoolhka. eehšakiciihamaani. waawiipisiaani. kweelamaka kiihkoneehsa. wiiyoonkonci kweelamaka kiihkoneehsa, niwiiwa  “ntotamawi!” iišita. paahpilotawita iišiteehiaani.
en: Just then it seemed as though someone had grabbed hold of my gigging pole. I became more afraid. I pushed back. I was in a hurry  and lost the fish. The reason I lost the fish, my wife told me “Ask  for it!” I think she was making fun of me.

mya: nkotanwi miišimaha kiyošia mihtohseenia meehtohkišwaata ahseema ceemonkaahkiita. “mehša, kiwaapamele kati” iilaata.
en: Once, a long time ago, an old Indian man would cut up tobacco and throw it in the water. “Grandfather, I want to see you”, he would say.

mya: noonki nipi leni weenteeki. peekamiiki. meencipiikanki. noonki neewaata lenipinšia. meešipiikanka. kiinwaakosita keepeeyaakwihšinki siipiiwi. seekisita. maacaamwita.
en: Then the water seemed to boil up. It got muddy. (The water) rose. Then he saw lenipinšia. He rose up. He was long, and stretched all the way across the river. He was scared. He ran away.

mya: alaankwa aancihseeta, mihtohseeniaki iilaacimwaaci, “lenipinšia aancihseewa”. iilaacimwaaci lenipinšia eehi kinoonki eehpyaata, ciinkwiali iši kati pakamikohsiikwi.
en: Whenever a star would change its place, the people would say “lenipinšia is moving”. They would say that lenipinšia was going where it was deep, so that thunder would not strike him.

mya: šiipaakana ntopalia eekimaawita myaamia.
en: Šiipaakana was a warrior and chief of the Myaamia.

mya: kiihkayonki ciikaahkwe weeyaahkita kweewihsita. nkotanwi kwiiwihsaki eeleeliiciki. kookiiciki aweena kati šiipi kookiita. ceeki kookiiciki naaninkoti moohkihsaaciki. šiipaakana teehši moohci moohkiiwaata. šiipi eehkawaahaaciki šišwici. sakanke maacaaciki. aacimwiciki šiipaakana eehkalaamwita.
en: When he was a boy he lived near Kiihkayonki (Fort Wayne). Once, some boys were bathing. They were diving to see who could dive the longest. They all dove, one after another, and came up quickly. Except for Šiipaakana, he didn’t come to the surface. For a long time they waited for him on the bank. Afterwards, they went home. They reported that Šiipaakana had drowned.

mya: eelaakwiki šiipaakana pyaata. neenki aatotanka. “kookiaani ceeki kiihkoneehsaki neemaani. ceeki kiikoo nipinki weeyaahkiciki neemaani. eehkonki neehpyaani miiwi neemaani. meetimiaani. wiikiaami neemaani. ahkwaanteeminki neepawiaani. ‘piintikiilo noohse’, iišita. peentikiaani. meehcikilita eewiiwiilita taahtakiihšinka. ‘alehši noohse neetomelaani. kiitimaakisiyani. myaalahoošiyani. kapootwe waaciinkwiiteeheeyani miihkweelimihkani’. noontohsiaani ahkwaanteemi iišiteehiaani. nipi saakaciwiaani.”
en: In the evening, Šiipaakana came. He told what he saw. “When I dove I saw all the fish. I saw everything that lives in the water. When I came to the bottom, I saw a road. I followed it. I saw a house. I stood at the door. “Come in, my grandchild”, someone said to me. I went in. A big beast with horns was lying down. ‘Only for this have I called you, my grandchild. You are pitiful. You will receive mercy from me. Whenever you are in trouble, remember me.’ Then I went out the door, I think. I came out of the water.”

mya: meehci kweewita maamiikaahkiita. ntopaliaki tipilahataakani keepeehšinaanki kaanseenseesiipi. mihšimaalhsaki miikaalakinta. mihšimaalhsaki neewinaašiciki. peeyankamwiaanki. anemaakaki ‘eenkihenta’ iišiteehiaanki. naahpa keepeehšinaanki šiipaakana šišwici neepawita. šiipaakana iilweeci: “ciikaahkwe keelišiwiciki. maamihšihka eehtimiciki. noonki ceemonkihsaani. peemicimiaani ‘nintahkalaamwi kati’ iišiteehiaani. noonki meehkwiteehiaani nimehšooma iišimita: ‘kiwiiciilamele kati’. meehkweelimaka. kiikoolaami eempinita. mayaawi keepeeyohšita. šišwici saakaciwiaani.”
en: Once he was a young man, he was a warrior. Us warriors were crossing the Ohio River on a raft. We were fighting the Americans. The Americans were chasing me. We got scattered. His comrades and I thought he had been killed. But when we crossed the river, Šiipaakana was standing on the bank. Šiipaakana said, “They were following me very closely. They almost caught up with me. Then I jumped into the water. While I was swimming I thought I would drown. Then I remembered what my grandfather told me: ‘I will help you’. I thought of him. Something lifted me up. He carried me straight across. I came out of the water onto the shore.”

mya: meehciweele šiipaakana weekimaata mahkoonsihkwali. nimacihsinwi siipiiwi šišwici weekita. iihkiyošiwita noonki keekiipihšita. noonki ‘keekiiphšia’ iilaaciki.
en: Later, Šiipaakana married Mahkoonsihkwa. He lived on the bank of the Mississinewa river. Then, when he was an old man, he became deaf. Then he was called ‘Keekiiphšia’ (Deaf Man).

mya: ninkiiki ooniini iilweewaaci. weentamawiciki.
en: This is what my mothers said. They told me about it.

mya: ninkya amihsali neehkimwicili-hkwa eehkweehsintehsiwici. yaalanwi peepoonweeta ninkiili aayoolhka. naapiinkwiaki niiyaaciki, nipilikoci kati ninkya amihsali. kiikoo-hkwa miilaaciki. miilaawaahsiikwili mooyahokociki.
en: My mother’s sister used to have seizures when she was becoming a young woman. She was five years older than my mother. The shamans went there to treat my aunt. People would give them something. Whenever they didn’t give them something, (the shamans) would throw shit at them.

mya: naapiinkwiaki šaawanwaki eeloolaaciki nipilaawaaci kati. naapiinkwiaki peentikalaaciki wiikiaami eehi nipilaawaaci. pootaweeciki alaaminkonci wiikiaami pahsaahkaha alakiihkwi. ninkya amihsali meehšišaakinaaciki akootayi teehši. neehkahatoonta eekotenkia awiilhsa mihtahkiši.
en: They hired some Shawnee shamans to treat her. The shamans led her inside the house where they were going to treat her. In the middle of the house they made a fire of tree bark. They stripped my aunt naked except for a breech-cloth. Her hair was untied, and it hung down.

mya: noonki naahkipioni ceenkweepihaaciki. noonki weelikaaciki. keewahtekaaciki koteewi. peepakihšiki neeweekaata mihtami koteewi kwaapahanki. peepakihšiki eeyooki koteewi maahanki. antepikaninki eehkwaahkawaata koteewi. ceeki awiilwa koteewi eehkwaahkawaaciki antepikaninki.
en: Now they sat her down on a stool. Then they began to dance. They danced around the fire. The one who led the dance first scooped up the fire with a board. He used a board to shovel the fire. He threw fire on her head. They all threw fire on her head.

mya: ninkya amihsali keekiipiinkweepita. paakišiinkweepita. moohci ninkihkeelintansoo iišileniwaaci. ninkya iilweeci: “nimihsa šaakosonta iišiteehiaani”. seehkwiaani. ninkya eetaahpaahkaašita alookanenki. eekwaniinkweehšimita iši kati neewaahsiiwaki. awiilwa iilweewaaci moohci awiilhsi šaakoteehsiinoowi.
en: My aunt sat with her eyes shut. She sat still. I don’t know what they did. My mother said: “I think my sister is being burned”. I cried. My mother pulled me into her lap. She covered my face so I wouldn’t see them. What they said was that not a single one of her hairs was burned.

mya: peelakiita. moohci ansihke neehkimowa. neepika palaani-matene peepoonwici.
en: She got well. She never had seizures (again). She died when she was eighty years old.

mya: kaapia myaamia kiyošia niwiinsooni miilita. awiila mayaawi awiinsooni ‘waapanaakikaapwa’.
en: Kaapia, an old Myaamia man, gave me my name. His real name was ‘Waapanaakikaapwa’.

mya: mihtohseeniaki neetonamahowaaci, kiikoo eenkihtoowaaci, nkoti alenia meemaaciki. “nihsweehikolo” iilaaciki, “kaapeewilo”. oonaana alenia ‘kaapia’ iilinta.
en: When the people went hunting, whenever they killed anything, they chose one man: “Divide it up”, they tell him, “divide equally”. This man is called a ‘kaapia’.

mya: šayiipaawe kiintoohki peenaašinki kaapia meentanka. kweecimatooka “kwaniswa-nko, kwiiwihsa-nko?” ‘kwiiwihsa’ iilinta. “niwiinsoonahaa kati niwiinsooni”. iiniini wiiyoonkonci ‘waapanaakikaapwa’ iišinki. niila kapootwe ‘kaapia’ iišiciki. kaapia neepita iiniini šayiipaawe peenaašinki. kaapia iišimaata nišihsali pimweeyohtamwali. weentamawita.
en: The very morning I was born, Kaapia was sick. He asked, “is it a girl, is it a boy?” He was told it was a boy. “I’ll give him my name”. That’s why I’m called Waapanaakikaapwa. After a while I was called Kaapia. Kaapia died that morning that I was born. Kaapia told my uncle Pimweeyohtamwa. He told me about it.

mya: kiintoohki kweewiaani eewiiyomiaani. waayaahtanohkwiali weekimaka kiihkayonki. eehi oohsali akiili waayaahtanonki weeyaahkilici.
en: When I got to be a young man I got married. I married a Wea woman at Kiihkayonki (Fort Wayne). Her parents lived at Waayaahtanonki (Ouiatenon) .

mya: niiši iiyaayaanki niwiiwa mihsoolinki. waapaahšiikinki naaminwihsaanki. peehkonteeki neehpyaanki.
en: My wife and I went there in a canoe. We went down the Wabash. It was nighttime when we arrived there.

mya: naahpa šayiipaawe noontamaanki mitemhsa. ntopaliaki neehsinta. ‘nintankihaamina’ iišiteeheeciki. aapahkwihkišonta.
en: To our surprise in the morning we heard a woman. She had been captured by the warriors. They thought they had killed her. She had been scalped.

mya: waayaahtanwa akima šayiipaawe maawatoomaata akwiiwhsemahi. pyaaciki. aacimwiciki. eehi aacimowaaci ntopaliwaaci, akima ataahtaani peemawatooka. neeweeta kati miikaahkiiwaaci eehtinanka.
en: In the morning the chief of the Wea called his boys together. They came. They held a council. When they were deciding whether to go on the war-path, the chief passed the war club around. Whoever takes it will be the leader when they fight.

mya: akima ataahtaani peemawatooka. kaawilaweeciki. moohci ahtenamaakiita. keewahtohseeta. ceeki moohci ahtenamaakiita. noonki niila pyaalotawita. miilita ataahtaani. šiipi moohci nintahtinam. kapootwe iišiteehiaani. kiinte eewiiyomiaani. “myaašiteeheeta” iileelimiciki kati ahtenansiiwaane. meemaani. eelimaakiaanki kati miikaahkiaanki. keeleešiwakinci neenkatohsiaanki.
en: The chief passed the war club around. They refused. None took it. He went around. Nobody would take it. Then he approached me. He offered me the war club. For a long time, I wouldn’t take it. I was thinking for a while. I had just gotten married. They would think I was a coward if I didn’t take the club. I took it. We got ready to leave and go fight. We followed the trail single-file.

mya: kapootwe neemaanki weešihenta tawaaninki ayaapiali. ninemaakaki: “keetwi iilaapyaahki? ayaapia mayaawi maamiikaahkia kiikaapwa. moošaki keeleešiwakinci, neewanswiaminciki moošaki. paamaka kitahtinaaminaan. aalwiteeheetaawi”, iišiciki.
en: After a while, we saw a buck drawn on a tree. My companions (said): “What’s the use? Buck is a real Kickapoo warrior. Every time we follow him, they would always get away from us. We’ll never catch him. Let’s give up”, they said.

mya: “eehinkaaši kati kiileešiwankwi” iilakiki.
en: “Let’s keep following him”, I said.

mya: kapootwe maayaahkweeki koteewi neemaanki. nkoti meemaka. neewiaanki peemitaacinkwiaanki. neewakinci koteenki ceenkweepiciki wiihsiniciki. aapweeyaanki.
en: After a while, at noon, we saw a fire. I took one person. We went ahead crawling. We saw them sitting around the fire eating. We went back.

mya: eehkawahakinci ninemaakinaanaki. pyaaciki. aacimwiaanki. “noonki paakwiitawaataawi”. “peehkonteeki ahkawaahtootaawi”. niila noonki, “miikaalaataawi eehkwi wiihsiniwaaci”.
en: We waited for our comrades. They came. We held a council. “Let’s attack now”. “Let’s wait til dark”. Then I said, “Let’s attack them while they’re eating”.

mya: noonki kaakiimohsiaanki. paakwiitawakinci. ceeki eenkihakinci nkoti teehši. ayaapia mayaawi šiinšiilaweeta. niiwi eensohkawaaciki kati sakiinaawaaci kati kihpilaawaaci. weenankaahkaalikociki.
en: Then we crept up. We attacked them. We killed all but one of them. Buck was very strong. Four people piled on top of him, to catch him and tie him up. He threw them off.

mya: kiyošia pyaata. “oowiši kwanak iihpinalinciki”. atahtawaanimi ahciwahi peekamaata. ahciwahi paapincinkiki.
en: An old man came up. “This is how they’re treated” (he said). He struck him on the arms with his club. His arms fell to his sides.

mya: noonki kiihpilakinci. “wiiteemiloome!” iilakinci. kaawilaweeta.
en: Now we tied him. “Come along with us”, we told him. He refused.

mya: noonki aapooši kiyošia pyaata. “oowiši kwanak iihpinalinciki”. seekilehšiweeholaata aneehciaapinti. eetaahpahaaciki. oošihsaata. neehkimwita. neepwaahkaata. aapooši “pyaalo!”
en: Again the old man came. “This is how they’re treated” (he said). He tied his bowstring around the man’s testicles. He pulled on it. He fell down. He fainted. He came to. Again (he was told) “come”.

mya: “moohci paamaka. moohci nimetimohsihsoo eehi kiikawaanki kati miloonihiyiikwi. oowaaha šaakoswiko.”
en: “No, never. I’m not some woman who you can torture in your home. Burn me here.”

mya: tawaaninki kiihpilaaciki. pootaweeciki. “miililo pwaakana!” iilaata. miilaaciki. eehpwaata eehkwi sahkahonta. eehpwaata eehkwi neehseeta. neehi ahpwaakanali paapincinkili atooninkonci.
en: They tied him to a stake. They started a fire. “Give me a pipe”, he said. They gave him one. He smoked the pipe as he was burned. He smoked as long as he was still breathing. Then the pipe fell from his mouth.

mya: ayaapia apwaaminki eesaahsonta. eewikaalinta ayaapiali. miišimaha aalinta mihtohseeniaki niiši-hkwa iišišiiniciki. eesaahsonciki ceeki teehtawaki aweehsaki alookayewaanki. moohci ninkihkiilimaahsoo kati eesaahsotiiwaata myaamiaki. moohci ansihke nineewaahsoo. ninoontansoo kati eesaahsonci myaamiaki.
en: Buck was tattooed on his thigh. A picture of a buck had been drawn on him. Long ago, that was the custom among some people. Their skins were tattooed with all kinds of animals. I don’t know whether the Myaamia would tattoo each other. I never saw them. I never heard that Myaamia would get tattooed.

mya: noohki neešonaminki kiihkayonki mihtohseenia neehsinta ntopaliahi eepahkwihkišonta. kaapia naašinki. “kiileešiwi!” iišinki. keeleešiwakiki.
en: The second time an Indian was captured at Kiihkayonki by a war party, he was scalped. I was fetched by Kaapia. “Follow him”, I was told. I followed them.

mya: šaaye eehkiileešiwaaciki ciikaahkwe eehi pimihkaweewaaci nipinki peekamiiki. neehi pimitaahkwihsenki eetahkohkiiciki. niiyaanci pimitaahkwihsenki eempihsaaciki. naanoohki eehinkaaha eehpankihšinkiki.
en: They followed them closely, to where the tracks went into the muddy water. Then they crossed on a footlog. From there they jumped off from the log. One after the other, they jumped down in the same place.

mya: kaapia neeweeta. eempihsaata. eehinkaaha eehpankihšinka. atahkiamoohi tawaanhsalwi kiintanankiki eehi eehpankihšinoowaata. eelaamicinki tawaanhsalwi ahkaatinki. aalweelita kati aayoolhka eehpyaaci. aalwiteeheeta.
en: Kaapia went first. He jumped down. He landed in the same place. His enemies had stuck a wooden arrow in the ground where they jumped down. The arrow hurt his foot. He couldn’t go any further. He gave up.

mya: iiniini ntaahsweni niišanwi teehši neetopalita kaapia iilweeci.
en: Kaapia said that he only went on the warpath those two times.

mya: waapimaankwa myaamia akima. aapooši miisaahakiaata ceemonkaahkaašiwia eelaaminaahiwia. kiihkeelimaka. kweewihsiaanki kiihkeelimaka.
en: Waapimaankwa was a Myaamia chief. He was also a missionary Baptist preacher. I knew him. I knew him since we were boys.

mya: waapaahšiikinki eehkoleenki amehšoomali pinšiwa eehinki waapaahšiikinki swaahteethsomatene piici pipoonwe eehpiši, eehi waalhkiinki mihsoola peempaaliki. pipyaawe miiwi peemihsenki. pipoonahkionkonci aniimhkikantaakanimi pinšiwa.
en: People used to receive payments at the Forks of the Wabash where his grandfather Pinšiwa was, at the Forks of the Wabash about seventy years ago, where the boats ran along the canal. A road ran alongside it. On the north side was Pinšiwa’s fence.

mya: niiyaahi tawaani meehswiki anikwa eehkwamaahkweeta, oonsaanikwa. wiihsa kwiiwhsaki ahsena peepakamaaciki, pinahwaawaaci kati. waapimaankwa weeciilweeta. awiila naapiši kati pakamaata. peminkiši aalaapita. ahseni paapintenki ahkiwaninki eehpiihsaata. šaakwikoleehona. neehpikikoleehona.
en: There a squirrel was climbing up a dead tree, a fox squirrel. Several boys were throwing rocks at him, trying to knock him off. Waapimaankwa was helping them. He wanted to hit it too. He looked up. A falling stone hit him on the nose. It mashed his nose. It made his nose bleed.

mya: iši piici mihtohseeniwiaani, aatotamoolaani kati.
en: This seems to be the way I’ve lived, and I’ll tell it to you.

mya: eehpiši meehtohseeniwiaani meeloohkamiki mataathswi-palaanaasi ntaahswaahkwe niiyomatene-niiwaasi pipoonwe. pahsaahkaha indiana nimehšooma ašiihkiwi iihkonanka. kiihkeelintaminki ‘mihšiinkweemiša’ noonki grant county iitaminki.
en: I was born in the spring of the year 1844. In the middle of Indiana my grandfather set aside a reservation. It is known as Mihšiinkweemiša (Burr Oak), in what is now called Grant County.

mya: niiyaahi neepwaaminki eekami kaahkiihkwe niiši iiyaayaani. niila nkoti neepwaankia. nihswi kiilhsooki neepwaaminki niiši iiyaayaani eekami nkoti pipoonwe. mitemhsa neepwaankia neepwaamita eekincikonki, eewikiinki, mahsenaakani kiilahkwatamenki, neehineenki, kiihkaapiikahikonki. poonineepwaaminki niišomatene peepoonwiaani. maawi meehciweele neepwaaminki. pilwišiši iiyaayaani neepwaaminkonci.
en: I went to school there every day. I (had) one teacher. I went to school there three months out of every year. A woman teacher taught me arithmetic, writing, reading, singing, and drawing. I quit school when I was twenty years old. That was the very end of my schooling. I went far away from the school.

mya: noonki ašiihkiwi meemaani, niiyaanci moonahamaani. ooneela atahkima nkotwaahkwe kaakaathsomateni kweetaahkonaminki. aalinta mihtehki. aasitawan tawaana meeneehwiki moonahamaani. ašiihkiwi neekawahkiki. niiyaanci ceeki kiikoo peehkiniikinki. niiyaaha eensiwatwaani miincipi, noohkimina, peniiki, leciiminiiki, ahseemaaki, kociihsaki, mihšiimišaahkwaki, eemihkwaana, iihkihtaminkia, kaayociikia, wiinhsiihsiaki, mihtahkatwa, šeekwaahkwahaminki, akaayomina, napaleeteeminiiki, makiinkweeminiiki, eehsipanimina, waawiyiihpiniiki, neehpikiciikia, ahsiimina, katoohwakimina, ateehimina, atehseeminiiki, papakimina, peeweeyociaki, myaalweehki, ahkaansa-pakaana, waapipakaana, barley neehi rye.
en: Then I bought some land, and from then on out I farmed it. The farm was 160 (acres). Part of it was wooded. I farmed the rest of it, where the trees were gone. The land was sandy. Because of that, everything grew well. There I planted corn, wheat, potatoes, peas, tobacco plants, beans, apple trees, pumpkins, watermelons, cucumbers, onions, hay, straw, gooseberries, raspberries, blackberries, currants, turnips, tomatoes, papaws, cherries, strawberries, plums, blackhaws, peaches, walnut trees, pecans, hickory nuts, barley, and rye.

mya: nihswi pipoonwe noonki eehkwi caaciiliteeki. nintašiihkiomi ceeki neemhkikanteeki, niimhkikantaakana eeyoonki. niišwi wiikiaama nintašiihkiominki. niišwi neekatikaašikaana niila eehtwaani, miincipikaani, noohkiminikaani, eewihakiki eehi wiikiwaaci, moonahikonki eeyoonkia teehsikaani, noonaakanaapowi wiikiaami. iišiteehiaani niiyomateni-yaalanwaasi nkoti acre iilakinteeki.
en: For three years now there’s been a drought. My land is all fenced off with fence rails. There are two houses on my land. I have two stables, a corn crib, a building for the wheat, a place where the tenants live, a shed for the farm tools, and a milk house. I think it totals 45 acres.

mya: nkoti kiihkišaakani noohkimini napale šooli iilakinteeki noonki niipinwe.
en: One bushel of wheat is worth half a dollar this summer.

mya: noohsina kiišikonki weeyaahkiyani meehceelimekwahki kiwiinsoonemi.
en: Our father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.
